This is a **support material** for Lesson 6. You do not need to run it in
the class - the lesson loads the dataset that this document creates
(`Data/dt_engineered.rds`). Read it if you want to see *why* every variable
looks the way it does, or if you want to reproduce the decisions on your own
data.

In Lesson 5 we adjusted variables by hand: merging categories, capping
numbers, banding. Here we do the same thing for **all** predictors in a
systematic way. For every variable we ask the same questions:

1.  Should it be a **category** or a **number**? (Numbers get one
    multiplier for a whole variable, categories one per level.)
2.  Which **adjustment** makes the signal clearer and the estimate more
    stable? (capping, merging, banding, transformation, truncating,
    rounding, replacing invalid values.)
3.  Does the adjusted variable bring **new information**, or is it noise?

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

```{r cell_01}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)
library(statmod)
options(scipen = 5)

# on Posit Cloud the project folder is /cloud/project, locally it is the folder above Support
proj <- if (dir.exists("/cloud/project")) "/cloud/project" else normalizePath("..")

source(file.path(proj, "Support/enforce_data_types.R"))
source(file.path(proj, "Support/rmse_group.R"))
source(file.path(proj, "Support/emb_chart_plotly.R"))
source(file.path(proj, "Support/tweedie_deviance.R"))
```

### Principles

-   **Decide on the training rows only.** Every choice below (the cap, the
    bands, the levels we merge) is made by looking at the *training* part of
    the Lesson 5 split. Validation rows are never used to decide, so they
    stay an honest test. The choices are then applied to *all* rows.
-   **Keep the original column, create a new one.** The originals stay in
    the dataset next to the engineered ones.
-   **Compare forms with the same yardstick.** Looking at a chart is
    necessary but not sufficient, so we also measure each form with a
    cross-validated Tweedie deviance (explained below).

### Data and the train / validation split

This is exactly the setup from Lesson 5: same data, same predictors, same
complete cases and the same seed, so we get the same training rows.

```{r cell_02}
dt_pol_w_claims <- readRDS(file.path(proj, "Data/dt_pol_w_claims_target.rds"))

var_types <- c(
  Year = "category", Time_on_book = "number", Customer_Type = "category",
  D_age = "number", D_age_banded = "category", BonusMalus = "number",
  D_ZIP = "category", VEH_type = "category", Veh_type1 = "category",
  Veh_type2 = "category", VEH_brand = "category", Construct_year = "number",
  Capacity = "number", Nr_of_seats = "category", Sum_insured = "number"
)

dt_pol_w_claims <- dt_pol_w_claims |>
  enforce_data_types(var_types)

n_before <- nrow(dt_pol_w_claims)
dt_pol_w_claims <- dt_pol_w_claims[complete.cases(dt_pol_w_claims[names(var_types)]), ]
c(rows_before = n_before, rows_after = nrow(dt_pol_w_claims))

set.seed(58742) # same seed as in Lesson 5

n_rows <- nrow(dt_pol_w_claims)
train_idx <- sample(n_rows, round(0.80 * n_rows)) # 80/20 split between train and valid

train <- dt_pol_w_claims[train_idx, ]
valid <- dt_pol_w_claims[-train_idx, ]
```

Rows with a missing value in any predictor are dropped, as in Lesson 5. It
is a tiny part of the data, and we do not want to invent values for them.

### The yardstick: cross-validated Tweedie deviance

To compare several forms of one variable we always fit the same model
`Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + <the variable in one form>` and measure how
much better it predicts than the vehicle-type-only model.

-   We use 5-fold cross-validation **inside the training data**: the model is
    fitted on 4/5 of the rows and scored on the remaining 1/5, five times.
-   The score is the **Tweedie deviance**, which is the loss the GLM itself
    optimises (see `Support/tweedie_deviance.R`). It uses every row. The
    grouped RMSE from Lesson 5 puts the rows into 5 groups first, which
    throws a lot of information away - see the last section for why this
    matters when the number of claims is small.
-   Reported as **gain in thousands**: deviance of the vehicle-only model
    minus deviance of the model with the variable. Bigger is better, a value
    around zero means "no new information", negative means the variable hurts
    on unseen data. The folds are repeated with 3 different seeds, `sd_k`
    shows how much the number moves with the fold assignment.

```{r cell_03}
glm_tweedie <- function(formula, data) {
  glm(
    formula = formula,
    data = data,
    family = statmod::tweedie(var.power = 1.5, link.power = 0),
    weights = Time_Exposure
  )
}

cv_deviance <- function(formula, data, seed = 1, k = 5) {
  set.seed(seed)
  fold <- sample(rep(seq_len(k), length.out = nrow(data)))
  total <- 0
  for (i in seq_len(k)) {
    fit <- glm_tweedie(formula, data[fold != i, ])
    held_out <- data[fold == i, ]
    total <- total + tweedie_deviance(
      held_out$Burning_Cost,
      predict(fit, held_out, type = "response"),
      held_out$Time_Exposure
    )
  }
  total
}

# a named list of formulas -> gain (in thousands) of each over the base formula
compare_forms <- function(forms, data = tr, base = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged, seeds = 1:3) {
  base_dev <- sapply(seeds, function(s) cv_deviance(base, data, s))
  n_base <- length(coef(glm_tweedie(base, data)))

  results <- lapply(names(forms), function(nm) {
    gain <- (base_dev - sapply(seeds, function(s) cv_deviance(forms[[nm]], data, s))) / 1000
    data.frame(
      form = nm,
      cv_gain_k = round(mean(gain), 1),
      sd_k = round(sd(gain), 1),
      extra_parameters = length(coef(glm_tweedie(forms[[nm]], data))) - n_base
    )
  })
  bind_rows(results)
}

# exposure share and exposure-weighted actual burning cost per level of a variable
level_table <- function(data, var) {
  data |>
    group_by(level = .data[[var]]) |>
    summarise(
      exposure_pct = round(100 * sum(Time_Exposure) / sum(data$Time_Exposure), 1),
      actual = round(weighted.mean(Burning_Cost, Time_Exposure)),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}
```

### Step 0: the target

The burning cost is `Ult_Loss / Time_Exposure`, so a moderate claim on a very
short policy turns into an enormous value. Let's look at the highest values
and at what a cap at a high percentile of the positive losses would do.

```{r cell_04}
train |>
  arrange(desc(Burning_Cost)) |>
  select(Time_Exposure, Ult_Loss, Burning_Cost) |>
  head(5)
```

```{r cell_05}
positive_bc <- train$Burning_Cost[train$Burning_Cost > 0]

cap_candidates <- lapply(c(0.95, 0.98, 0.99, 0.995, 0.999), function(p) {
  cap <- quantile(positive_bc, p)
  data.frame(
    percentile = 100 * p,
    cap = round(cap),
    rows_capped_train = sum(train$Burning_Cost > cap),
    rows_capped_valid = sum(valid$Burning_Cost > cap),
    loss_removed_pct = round(100 * (1 - sum(pmin(train$Burning_Cost, cap) * train$Time_Exposure) /
      sum(train$Burning_Cost * train$Time_Exposure)), 1)
  )
})
bind_rows(cap_candidates)
```

**Decision: cap at the 99.5th percentile of the positive burning cost,
computed on the training data.** Only a handful of rows are affected and
about 1% of the total loss is removed, so the nominal level of the target
(and the price level we compare with later) hardly changes. Such rows,
however, have a huge influence on squared errors, and they can make a
variable look good or bad by chance. The cap does not remove them, it just
limits their weight. A lower cap (95%, 98%) would remove 4-10% of the loss
and starts to change the risk we are trying to model.

The original column is kept as `Burning_Cost_raw`, the capped one replaces
`Burning_Cost`, so all helper functions from Lesson 5 work unchanged. A
caveat: from here on the RMSE values are **not comparable** with the Lesson 5
numbers, because the target is different.

```{r cell_06}
target_cap <- quantile(positive_bc, 0.995)
target_cap
```

The working copy of the training data `tr` is the one we use for all
investigations. It gets the capped target and the vehicle-type merge from
Lesson 5 (categories with almost no exposure go to the base category `CAR`).

```{r cell_07}
tr <- train |>
  mutate(
    Burning_Cost_raw = Burning_Cost,
    Burning_Cost = pmin(Burning_Cost, target_cap),
    Veh_type2_merged = ifelse(Veh_type2 %in% c("", "OTHER", "TRACTOR"), "CAR", Veh_type2)
  )

level_table(tr, "Veh_type2_merged")
```

Our baseline model is the vehicle type only. Its fitted values are what we
compare the actual burning cost with in the charts below - the same "unfitted
variable" charts as in Lesson 5: look for a clear trend of the **Actual**
line while the **Fitted** line is flat.

```{r cell_08}
base_model <- glm_tweedie(Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged, tr)
tr$pred <- predict(base_model, tr, type = "response")

look <- function(var) emb_chart_plotly(model = NULL, x_var = var, dt.frm = tr)
```

### BonusMalus

```{r cell_09}
look("BonusMalus")
```

```{r cell_10}
level_table(tr, "BonusMalus") |>
  filter(level %in% c(-1, 0, 1, 2, 12, 13, 14, 15))
```

What we see:

-   The actual burning cost falls steeply with the level, roughly by the
    same percentage per level (a straight line on the log scale) - a good
    candidate for a **number**.
-   Levels below zero (the worst claims history) are risky, but have almost
    no exposure.
-   **Level 0 is odd.** It holds over 10% of the exposure and its burning
    cost is tiny, while its neighbour level 1 is among the riskiest. It does
    not follow the trend at all, so it is most likely a placeholder (for
    example a default value for customers without a record) and not a
    "driver with no history". We do not know what it means in the source
    system.

If we feed `BonusMalus` as it is, level 0 sits at the "risky" end of the
scale but behaves like a very safe driver, and the single multiplier is
pulled towards zero. We want to keep **one column** (no extra flag), so we
replace the odd values with a level that behaves the same way: the burning
cost of level 0 is similar to the safest levels 12-14, so we recode **0 to
13**. Negative levels have a tiny exposure and a risk like the worst
positive levels, so we set them to 1.

```{r cell_11}
tr <- tr |>
  mutate(
    BM_recoded = ifelse(BonusMalus < 0, 1, ifelse(BonusMalus == 0, 13, BonusMalus)),
    BM_recoded_8 = ifelse(BonusMalus < 0, 1, ifelse(BonusMalus == 0, 8, BonusMalus)),
    BM_band = cut(
      BonusMalus,
      breaks = c(-Inf, -1, 0, 2, 5, 8, 11, 13, Inf),
      labels = c("<0", "0", "1-2", "3-5", "6-8", "9-11", "12-13", "14+")
    )
  )

compare_forms(list(
  "number as is" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + BonusMalus,
  "number, negatives -> 1, 0 -> 13" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + BM_recoded,
  "number, negatives -> 1, 0 -> 8" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + BM_recoded_8,
  "number, log of the recoded level" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + log(BM_recoded),
  "8 bands (0 and negatives separate)" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + BM_band
))
```

**Decision: `BonusMalus_adj` - a number, negatives to 1 and 0 to 13.** The
raw number is by far the worst numeric form. The recoded one is almost as
good as the 8 bands, which fit each band separately but need 7 extra
parameters. The recoded number needs just one and the interpretation is
simple: *each level up multiplies the expected burning cost by exp(beta)*.
The log of the level is worse - a log link already means "constant
percentage per level", a log of the level would mean "constant percentage
per doubling of the level", which is not what the chart shows.

One honest consequence: the model can no longer tell a 0 from a real 13.
That is a trade-off we accept to keep a simple numeric variable.

### Time_on_book

```{r cell_12}
tr <- tr |> mutate(Time_on_book_look = pmin(Time_on_book, 12))
look("Time_on_book_look")
```

The burning cost falls with the years with the company, but there are only a
few years with a decent exposure. Beyond year 10 the exposure is tiny, the
actual values jump around (and a few tail values are extreme).

```{r cell_13}
tr <- tr |>
  mutate(
    TOB_cap8 = pmin(Time_on_book, 8),
    TOB_cap10 = pmin(Time_on_book, 10),
    TOB_band = factor(pmin(Time_on_book, 4)),
    TOB_cat = factor(pmin(Time_on_book, 11))
  )

compare_forms(list(
  "number as is" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + Time_on_book,
  "number, capped at 8" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + TOB_cap8,
  "number, capped at 10" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + TOB_cap10,
  "log, as is" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + log(Time_on_book),
  "log, capped at 10" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + log(TOB_cap10),
  "bands 1 / 2 / 3 / 4+" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + TOB_band,
  "every year 1-10, 11+ separately" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + TOB_cat
))
```

**Decision: `Time_on_book_cap` - a number capped at 8.** Once the tail is
capped, a linear term, a log and bands are practically indistinguishable, so
we choose the simplest to explain: one multiplier per extra year. The
uncapped number is the only form that does not help - the thin tail pulls
the line. A log is not needed for an integer variable with eight useful
values; it does the same job as the cap (it squeezes the tail) and makes the
interpretation harder (a multiplier per *doubling* of the years).

The actual values go up a little between year 2 and 3, so a flexible form
could follow it. We deliberately choose a monotonic form: it is what a
business partner expects, and the difference in fit is small.

### Sum_insured

```{r cell_14}
summary(train$Sum_insured)
n_distinct(train$Sum_insured)
```

This variable has more than 20 000 different values in the training data, so
no value has any real exposure and a chart by value is just noise. To see
the trend we need to **discretize it first**. Value 0 is not a valid sum
insured, so we replace it with the median of the positive values.

```{r cell_15}
si_median <- median(train$Sum_insured[train$Sum_insured > 0])
si_median

tr <- tr |>
  mutate(
    SI_fixed = ifelse(Sum_insured <= 0, si_median, Sum_insured),
    SI_band = cut(
      SI_fixed,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 2000, 4000, 6000, 8000, 10000, 15000, 20000, 30000, 50000, Inf),
      labels = c("<=2k", "2-4k", "4-6k", "6-8k", "8-10k", "10-15k", "15-20k", "20-30k", "30-50k", "50k+")
    )
  )

look("SI_band")
```

The burning cost grows with the insured value, fast at the beginning, then
more slowly. The few policies above 30 000 have almost no exposure. This
shape (steep first, flat later) is typical for a transformation like a **log**.

```{r cell_16}
tr <- tr |>
  mutate(
    SI_thousand = Sum_insured / 1000,
    SI_fixed_thousand = SI_fixed / 1000,
    SI_cap30_thousand = pmin(SI_fixed, 30000) / 1000,
    SI_log = log(SI_fixed)
  )

compare_forms(list(
  "number as is (thousands)" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + SI_thousand,
  "number, 0 -> median" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + SI_fixed_thousand,
  "number, 0 -> median, capped at 30k" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + SI_cap30_thousand,
  "log, 0 -> median" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + SI_log,
  "10 bands" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + SI_band
))
```

**Decision: `Sum_insured_log` - the log of the sum insured, with 0 replaced
by the median.** It is the best form and a single parameter, and the log
makes a separate cap unnecessary. The interpretation: *doubling the sum
insured multiplies the expected burning cost by 2^beta*. We keep a banded
copy, `Sum_insured_band`, only for charts (a numeric column with thousands
of values cannot be plotted by value).

### Capacity

```{r cell_17}
summary(train$Capacity)
n_distinct(train$Capacity)
```

Engine capacity has 883 values (in cm3), a few are 0 (invalid) and a few are
extreme. Same approach as before: discretize to see the shape.

```{r cell_18}
capacity_median <- median(train$Capacity[train$Capacity > 0])
capacity_median

tr <- tr |>
  mutate(
    CAP_fixed = ifelse(Capacity <= 0, capacity_median, Capacity),
    CAP_look = cut(
      CAP_fixed,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 800, 1000, 1200, 1300, 1400, 1500, 1600, 1800, 2000, 2500, 3000, Inf)
    )
  )

look("CAP_look")
```

The shape is **not monotonic**: small engines are cheap, the middle range
(1300-1500) is relatively risky, then it drops, and the large engines are
the riskiest. A straight line (or a log) cannot follow this, but a handful of
bands can.

```{r cell_19}
cap_labels <- c("<=1000", "1001-1300", "1301-1600", "1601-2000", "2001-3000", "3000+")

tr <- tr |>
  mutate(
    CAP_band = cut(CAP_fixed, breaks = c(-Inf, 1000, 1300, 1600, 2000, 3000, Inf), labels = cap_labels),
    CAP_clipped = pmin(pmax(CAP_fixed, 800), 4000)
  )

compare_forms(list(
  "number as is" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + Capacity,
  "number, clipped to 800-4000" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + CAP_clipped,
  "log, clipped to 800-4000" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + log(CAP_clipped),
  "log, as is" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + log(CAP_fixed),
  "6 bands" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + CAP_band
))
```

**Decision: `Capacity_band` - 6 bands, with 0 replaced by the median.** The
bands follow the irregular shape and beat all numeric forms. The log of the
unclipped value is the only form that clearly hurts: a few extreme capacities
dominate the single coefficient. If you prefer a number for its simplicity,
the clipped log is the best numeric alternative.

### Construct_year

```{r cell_20}
tr <- tr |> mutate(Construct_year_look = pmax(Construct_year, 2000))
look("Construct_year_look")
```

Almost all exposure sits in 2007-2015. Older cars have a few percent of the
exposure and noisy values, and the actual burning cost in the main range
has no clear trend. That is a weak variable. Let's see whether any form
rescues it.

```{r cell_21}
tr <- tr |>
  mutate(
    CY_capped = pmin(pmax(Construct_year, 2007), 2015),
    CY_cat = factor(pmin(pmax(Construct_year, 2006), 2015)),
    CY_band = factor(
      ifelse(Construct_year <= 2006, "<=2006", ifelse(Construct_year <= 2010, "2007-2010", "2011+")),
      levels = c("<=2006", "2007-2010", "2011+")
    )
  )

compare_forms(list(
  "number as is" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + Construct_year,
  "number, capped to 2007-2015" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + CY_capped,
  "every year 2006-2015 separately" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + CY_cat,
  "3 bands" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + CY_band
))
```

**Decision: `Construct_year_band` - 3 bands (up to 2006, 2007-2010, 2011+).**
No numeric form helps (the trend is not a straight line), every year
separately is too noisy, and the 3 bands catch the one thing that is there
- a difference between old and newer cars. The gain is small, so this is a
candidate that a variable selection should treat with suspicion.

### Nr_of_seats

```{r cell_22}
level_table(tr, "Nr_of_seats")
```

The variable contains impossible values (115, 999, 201, ...) with a near
zero exposure. Most of the exposure is on 5 (the base) and 2 seats. We first
send the impossible values and everything above 9 to the base category 5.

```{r cell_23}
tr <- tr |>
  mutate(
    NS_clean = ifelse(Nr_of_seats %in% as.character(1:9), Nr_of_seats, "5"),
    NS_number = as.numeric(NS_clean),
    NS_group = factor(
      case_when(
        NS_clean == "2" ~ "2",
        NS_clean == "3" ~ "3",
        NS_clean %in% c("7", "8", "9") ~ "7+",
        TRUE ~ "1/4/5/6"
      ),
      levels = c("2", "3", "1/4/5/6", "7+")
    )
  )

compare_forms(list(
  "number 1-9" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + NS_number,
  "every level 1-9 separately" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + NS_clean,
  "4 groups: 2 / 3 / 1,4,5,6 / 7+" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + NS_group
))
```

Notice the row for every level separately: the deviance punishes a model that
predicts (almost) zero for a group where a claim later appears. A level with
very few policies and no claims gets a coefficient far below the rest, and
the held-out claim that falls in it ruins the score. This is why levels with
a tiny exposure must be merged.

**Decision: `Nr_of_seats_grp` - 4 groups (2, 3, 7+, and 1/4/5/6 including the
cleaned values).** The gain is practically zero. The seat groups overlap with
the vehicle type (for example 72% of the exposure of 3-seat vehicles are
pickups), so part of the information is already in the model. Keeping the
variable in the dataset is useful: a variable selection should not pick it.

### Vehicle type, driver age, brand, ZIP and the rest

Vehicle types are the base of every model, so we keep the merge from Lesson 5
(`Veh_type2_merged`). The other classifications of the vehicle (`Veh_type1`,
`VEH_type`) have many tiny levels: we group the levels with less than 1% of
exposure into `other`.

**D_age** - a first look at the exposure:

```{r cell_24}
tr |>
  group_by(D_age) |>
  summarise(
    exposure_pct = round(100 * sum(Time_Exposure) / sum(tr$Time_Exposure), 1),
    actual = round(weighted.mean(Burning_Cost, Time_Exposure)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(exposure_pct)) |>
  head(6)
```

Ages 43-46 together hold more than half of the exposure. That is not how real
driver ages are distributed, so these look like a default or imputed value
and not true ages - we do not know the source. It limits what any form of this
variable can achieve, because most of the portfolio sits at one point. The
oldest and youngest drivers have very little exposure, so we clip the age.

```{r cell_25}
tr <- tr |>
  mutate(
    AGE_clipped = pmin(pmax(D_age, 25), 80),
    AGE_band = cut(D_age, breaks = c(-Inf, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, Inf))
  )

compare_forms(list(
  "number as is" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + D_age,
  "number, clipped to 25-80" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + AGE_clipped,
  "number, clipped + squared term" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + AGE_clipped + I(AGE_clipped^2),
  "bands 30 / 40 / 50 / 60 / 70" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + AGE_band
))
```

**Decision: `D_age_adj` - the age clipped to 25-80, as a number.** No form
helps, so this is the "best effort" version: a harmless one, kept so that
the variable selection has something to reject.

**VEH_brand** has 126 levels and most of them have a tiny exposure. We group
the brands under a minimum exposure share into `other`; the question is how
high the threshold should be.

```{r cell_26}
# the levels that have at least `min_pct` % of the training exposure
levels_to_keep <- function(x, weight, min_pct) {
  share <- tapply(weight, x, sum) / sum(weight) * 100
  names(share)[share >= min_pct]
}

group_rare <- function(x, keep) ifelse(x %in% keep, x, "other")

tr <- tr |>
  mutate(
    BRAND_05 = group_rare(VEH_brand, levels_to_keep(VEH_brand, Time_Exposure, 0.5)),
    BRAND_1 = group_rare(VEH_brand, levels_to_keep(VEH_brand, Time_Exposure, 1)),
    BRAND_2 = group_rare(VEH_brand, levels_to_keep(VEH_brand, Time_Exposure, 2))
  )

c(brands = n_distinct(tr$VEH_brand), levels_05 = n_distinct(tr$BRAND_05),
  levels_1 = n_distinct(tr$BRAND_1), levels_2 = n_distinct(tr$BRAND_2))

compare_forms(list(
  "brands under 0.5% -> other" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + BRAND_05,
  "brands under 1% -> other" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + BRAND_1,
  "brands under 2% -> other" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + BRAND_2
))
```

The more levels we keep, the worse it gets: each brand estimate is noisy, and
the noise costs more than the real differences between brands gain.
**Decision: `VEH_brand_grp` - brands under 2% exposure to `other`.** Merging
by *similar risk* (instead of by exposure) is also possible, but with brands
of this size we would be fitting noise, so we keep the simple rule.

**D_ZIP** has 554 four-digit codes. The Lesson 5 hint was to **truncate** it:

```{r cell_27}
tr <- tr |>
  mutate(
    ZIP_1 = substr(D_ZIP, 1, 1),
    ZIP_2 = group_rare(substr(D_ZIP, 1, 2), levels_to_keep(substr(D_ZIP, 1, 2), Time_Exposure, 0.5)),
    ZIP_3 = group_rare(substr(D_ZIP, 1, 3), levels_to_keep(substr(D_ZIP, 1, 3), Time_Exposure, 0.5))
  )

compare_forms(list(
  "first digit" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + ZIP_1,
  "first 2 digits (rare -> other)" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + ZIP_2,
  "first 3 digits (rare -> other)" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + ZIP_3
))
```

The finer the region, the worse. **Decision: `D_ZIP_1` - the first digit.** The
region has no visible effect in our data at any level of detail, so the
coarsest version is the safest.

**The rest:** `Year` and `Customer_Type` are used as they are (4 and 2
levels); `Veh_type1` and `VEH_type` get the same grouping of levels under 1%
exposure.

```{r cell_28}
tr <- tr |>
  mutate(
    V1_grp = group_rare(Veh_type1, levels_to_keep(Veh_type1, Time_Exposure, 1)),
    VT_grp = group_rare(VEH_type, levels_to_keep(VEH_type, Time_Exposure, 1))
  )

compare_forms(list(
  "Year" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + Year,
  "Customer_Type" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + Customer_Type,
  "Veh_type1, levels under 1% -> other" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + V1_grp,
  "VEH_type, levels under 1% -> other" = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + VT_grp
))
```

None of them adds information beyond the vehicle type.

### The final function and the dataset

All decisions in one place. A single function creates all the columns, so
that training and validation data (and any future data) are guaranteed to be
treated in exactly the same way. Everything that was *learned* from the data
(the cap, the medians, the lists of frequent levels) is computed on the
training rows and passed in as `fe_params`.

```{r cell_29}
fe_params <- list(
  target_cap = target_cap,
  si_median = si_median,
  capacity_median = capacity_median,
  brands_keep = levels_to_keep(train$VEH_brand, train$Time_Exposure, 2),
  veh1_keep = levels_to_keep(train$Veh_type1, train$Time_Exposure, 1),
  veh_type_keep = levels_to_keep(train$VEH_type, train$Time_Exposure, 1)
)

add_features <- function(df, fe) {
  df |>
    mutate(
      # target: keep the original, cap the extreme values
      Burning_Cost_raw = Burning_Cost,
      Burning_Cost = pmin(Burning_Cost, fe$target_cap),

      # vehicle type (Lesson 5): categories with (almost) no exposure to the base category
      Veh_type2_merged = ifelse(Veh_type2 %in% c("", "OTHER", "TRACTOR"), "CAR", Veh_type2),

      # BonusMalus: negatives -> 1 (worst), the odd level 0 -> 13, then used as a number
      BonusMalus_adj = ifelse(BonusMalus < 0, 1, ifelse(BonusMalus == 0, 13, BonusMalus)),

      # Time_on_book: number, capped at 8 (little exposure above)
      Time_on_book_cap = pmin(Time_on_book, 8),

      # Sum_insured: invalid 0 -> median, log; the band is for charts only
      Sum_insured_log = log(ifelse(Sum_insured <= 0, fe$si_median, Sum_insured)),
      Sum_insured_band = cut(
        ifelse(Sum_insured <= 0, fe$si_median, Sum_insured),
        breaks = c(-Inf, 2000, 4000, 6000, 8000, 10000, 15000, 20000, 30000, 50000, Inf),
        labels = c("<=2k", "2-4k", "4-6k", "6-8k", "8-10k", "10-15k", "15-20k", "20-30k", "30-50k", "50k+")
      ),

      # Capacity: invalid 0 -> median, then 6 bands (the shape is not monotonic)
      Capacity_band = cut(
        ifelse(Capacity <= 0, fe$capacity_median, Capacity),
        breaks = c(-Inf, 1000, 1300, 1600, 2000, 3000, Inf),
        labels = c("<=1000", "1001-1300", "1301-1600", "1601-2000", "2001-3000", "3000+")
      ),

      # Construct_year: 3 bands
      Construct_year_band = factor(
        ifelse(Construct_year <= 2006, "<=2006", ifelse(Construct_year <= 2010, "2007-2010", "2011+")),
        levels = c("<=2006", "2007-2010", "2011+")
      ),

      # Nr_of_seats: impossible values -> base (5), then 4 groups
      Nr_of_seats_grp = factor(
        case_when(
          !(Nr_of_seats %in% as.character(1:9)) ~ "1/4/5/6",
          Nr_of_seats == "2" ~ "2",
          Nr_of_seats == "3" ~ "3",
          Nr_of_seats %in% c("7", "8", "9") ~ "7+",
          TRUE ~ "1/4/5/6"
        ),
        levels = c("2", "3", "1/4/5/6", "7+")
      ),

      # D_age: clipped, no form of this variable helps (best effort)
      D_age_adj = pmin(pmax(D_age, 25), 80),
      # banded copy of the age, for charts only (a chart by every age value would be just noise)
      D_age_chart = cut(D_age_adj, breaks = c(0, 30, 40, 45, 50, 60, 70, Inf)),

      # VEH_brand: brands under 2% of the training exposure -> other
      VEH_brand_grp = ifelse(VEH_brand %in% fe$brands_keep, VEH_brand, "other"),

      # Year is already a category (enforce_data_types above), so it needs no conversion here

      # D_ZIP: first digit
      D_ZIP_1 = substr(D_ZIP, 1, 1),

      # other classifications of the vehicle: levels under 1% -> other
      Veh_type1_grp = ifelse(Veh_type1 %in% fe$veh1_keep, Veh_type1, "other"),
      VEH_type_grp = ifelse(VEH_type %in% fe$veh_type_keep, VEH_type, "other")
    )
}
```

```{r cell_30}
dt_engineered <- dt_pol_w_claims |>
  mutate(Dataset = ifelse(row_number() %in% train_idx, "train", "valid")) |>
  add_features(fe_params)

# the function gives the same columns as the step by step investigation above
train_fe <- dt_engineered[train_idx, ] # same rows and the same order as `tr`
stopifnot(
  nrow(train_fe) == nrow(tr),
  all.equal(train_fe$Burning_Cost, tr$Burning_Cost),
  all.equal(train_fe$BonusMalus_adj, tr$BM_recoded),
  all.equal(train_fe$Time_on_book_cap, tr$TOB_cap8),
  all.equal(train_fe$Sum_insured_log, tr$SI_log),
  all(as.character(train_fe$Capacity_band) == as.character(tr$CAP_band)),
  all(as.character(train_fe$Construct_year_band) == as.character(tr$CY_band)),
  all(as.character(train_fe$Nr_of_seats_grp) == as.character(tr$NS_group)),
  all.equal(train_fe$D_age_adj, tr$AGE_clipped),
  all(train_fe$VEH_brand_grp == tr$BRAND_2),
  all(train_fe$D_ZIP_1 == tr$ZIP_1)
)
dim(dt_engineered)
```

The `Dataset` column stores which rows are training and which validation rows,
so the lesson uses exactly the split that all the decisions were made on.

#### Summary of the decisions

The gain is again the cross-validated deviance gain on the training data, now
computed on the final columns of the dataset.

```{r cell_31}
final_forms <- list(
  BonusMalus_adj = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + BonusMalus_adj,
  Time_on_book_cap = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + Time_on_book_cap,
  Sum_insured_log = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + Sum_insured_log,
  Capacity_band = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + Capacity_band,
  Construct_year_band = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + Construct_year_band,
  Nr_of_seats_grp = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + Nr_of_seats_grp,
  D_age_adj = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + D_age_adj,
  VEH_brand_grp = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + VEH_brand_grp,
  D_ZIP_1 = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + D_ZIP_1,
  Year = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + Year,
  Customer_Type = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + Customer_Type,
  Veh_type1_grp = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + Veh_type1_grp,
  VEH_type_grp = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + VEH_type_grp
)

decision_table <- data.frame(
  form = names(final_forms),
  type = c(
    "number", "number", "number (log)", "category", "category", "category", "number",
    "category", "category", "category", "category", "category", "category"
  ),
  adjustment = c(
    "negatives -> 1, odd level 0 -> 13",
    "capped at 8",
    "invalid 0 -> median, log",
    "invalid 0 -> median, 6 bands",
    "3 bands",
    "impossible values -> base, 4 groups",
    "clipped to 25-80",
    "brands under 2% exposure -> other",
    "first digit only",
    "as is",
    "as is",
    "levels under 1% -> other",
    "levels under 1% -> other"
  )
)

decision_table |>
  left_join(compare_forms(final_forms, data = train_fe), by = "form") |>
  rename(column = form) |>
  arrange(desc(cv_gain_k))
```

Reading the table:

-   **BonusMalus** carries by far the most information, then a group of
    clearly useful but much weaker variables: Time_on_book, Sum_insured,
    Capacity and Construct_year.
-   The rest is at or below zero even in the best form we found. We keep these
    variables in the dataset on purpose: a variable selection method should be
    able to leave them out, and a student should see what "no information"
    looks like.
-   The **numeric** variables - BonusMalus, Time_on_book and Sum_insured - are
    the ones where a single multiplier describes the effect, which is what makes
    a simple rating formula possible.

#### Bottom line per variable

The same table in words. The gain is the cross-validated deviance gain (in
thousands) over the vehicle-type-only model, from the table above. Exercise 1
shows a shorter version of this list.

-   **Veh_type2_merged (the base, category).** The vehicle type from Lesson 5,
    with the categories without exposure (blank, `OTHER`, `TRACTOR`) merged into
    `CAR`. It is in every model, so it has no gain of its own.
-   **BonusMalus_adj (number, gain 325).** Negatives to 1, the odd level 0 to
    13. By far the strongest variable, and the only one where a single
    multiplier per level is a clear, large effect.
-   **Sum_insured_log (number, gain 13).** Invalid 0 replaced by the median,
    then the log. A weak but real effect: a higher insured value means a higher
    burning cost, strongest at the low end.
-   **Time_on_book_cap (number, gain 13).** Capped at 8 years. Similar in
    strength to the sum insured: customers with the company longer have a
    lower burning cost.
-   **Capacity_band (category, gain 9).** Invalid 0 replaced by the median,
    then 6 bands. The effect is not monotonic, which is why it is a category and
    not a number. It costs 5 extra parameters for a modest gain.
-   **Construct_year_band (category, gain 6).** 3 bands. A small difference
    between older and newer cars; the least convincing of the "useful" group.
-   **Nr_of_seats_grp (category, gain 1).** Impossible values to the base,
    4 groups. Practically no new information, because the seats overlap with the
    vehicle type.
-   **D_age_adj (number, gain -0.3).** Clipped to 25-80. No form helps (most
    of the exposure sits at a few ages that look like a default value).
-   **Year (category, gain -0.9).** Used as it is (4 levels). No information
    beyond the vehicle type.
-   **Customer_Type (category, gain -1.3).** Used as it is. No information
    beyond the vehicle type.
-   **D_ZIP_1 (category, gain -2.7).** First digit of the ZIP only. The finer
    the region, the worse it gets; the first digit is the safest form.
-   **VEH_brand_grp (category, gain -3.3).** Brands under 2% exposure to
    `other`. Even after grouping, each brand estimate is more noise than signal.
-   **Veh_type1_grp and VEH_type_grp (category, gain -3.4 and -3.6).** Levels
    under 1% exposure to `other`. Other classifications of the same vehicle, so
    nothing new next to `Veh_type2_merged`.

A negative gain does not mean the variable is "bad" in general: it means that
on unseen data the extra parameters cost more than they bring. The variables
at the bottom are in the dataset on purpose, so a selection method has
something to reject. (One consequence you will see in Exercise 1: a method that
looks at the training data only can still pick one of them, because on the
training data a variable never makes the fit worse.)

### Save the dataset

```{r cell_32}
saveRDS(dt_engineered, file.path(proj, "Data/dt_engineered.rds"))
```

### Appendix: choosing between models - deviance and grouped RMSE

The grouped RMSE from Lesson 5 compares the average actual and predicted
burning cost in 5 groups of the validation data. It is the right picture for
"do the group averages match reality?", but with about 360 claims in the
validation set it is a coarse number for telling close models apart, and it
can even prefer a model without a variable we know is useful. Let's see it on 20 random 80/20 splits
of the data: we add `BonusMalus_adj` (the strongest variable) to the
vehicle-type-only model and check how often each metric says "better", with
and without the cap on the target.

```{r cell_33}
splits <- lapply(1:20, function(s) {
  set.seed(1000 + s)
  idx <- sample(nrow(dt_engineered), round(0.8 * nrow(dt_engineered)))
  tr_s <- dt_engineered[idx, ]
  va_s <- dt_engineered[-idx, ]

  bind_rows(lapply(c("no cap", "cap at 99.5%"), function(cap_nm) {
    if (cap_nm == "cap at 99.5%") {
      cap_s <- quantile(tr_s$Burning_Cost_raw[tr_s$Burning_Cost_raw > 0], 0.995)
      tr_s$Burning_Cost <- pmin(tr_s$Burning_Cost_raw, cap_s)
      va_s$Burning_Cost <- pmin(va_s$Burning_Cost_raw, cap_s)
    } else {
      tr_s$Burning_Cost <- tr_s$Burning_Cost_raw
      va_s$Burning_Cost <- va_s$Burning_Cost_raw
    }

    m_base <- glm_tweedie(Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged, tr_s)
    m_bm <- glm_tweedie(Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2_merged + BonusMalus_adj, tr_s)
    p_base <- predict(m_base, va_s, type = "response")
    p_bm <- predict(m_bm, va_s, type = "response")

    data.frame(
      split = s,
      target = cap_nm,
      rmse_base = rmse_group(va_s$Burning_Cost, p_base, va_s$Time_Exposure, 5),
      rmse_with_bm = rmse_group(va_s$Burning_Cost, p_bm, va_s$Time_Exposure, 5),
      dev_base = tweedie_deviance(va_s$Burning_Cost, p_base, va_s$Time_Exposure),
      dev_with_bm = tweedie_deviance(va_s$Burning_Cost, p_bm, va_s$Time_Exposure)
    )
  }))
})

bind_rows(splits) |>
  group_by(target) |>
  summarise(
    rmse_base_mean = round(mean(rmse_base), 1),
    rmse_base_sd = round(sd(rmse_base), 1),
    splits_where_grouped_rmse_improves_pct = round(100 * mean(rmse_with_bm < rmse_base)),
    splits_where_deviance_improves_pct = round(100 * mean(dev_with_bm < dev_base))
  )
```

What to take from the table:

-   The **cap** reduces the spread of the validation RMSE only a little - it
    is a cheap safeguard, not a cure.
-   **BonusMalus** is by far the best variable in the data, yet the grouped RMSE
    says that adding it makes the model *worse* in almost every split. The
    deviance says "better" in every split.
-   That is why Lesson 6 compares and selects variables with the deviance, which
    uses every row. The grouped RMSE keeps its place as the intuitive, visual
    check of the chosen model (the lift chart and the pooling idea from Lesson
    5); it is just not the number to pick between close models with.
